name: Dan Flavin
bio: Dan Flavin (1933–1996) made art from commercially available fluorescent tubes, in standard lengths and a limited range of colours. His first such work, the diagonal of May 25, 1963 (to Constantin Brancusi), was a single gold tube fixed at an angle to a wall. From then on he arranged tubes and fixtures in corners, across corridors and through whole buildings, letting coloured light flood the surrounding space. He dedicated many works to friends and artists, including the long series of 'monuments' for V. Tatlin. Late works include a church in Milan (Santa Maria Annunciata in Chiesa Rossa), Richmond Hall at the Menil Collection in Houston, and six buildings at the Chinati Foundation in Marfa, all completed around the time of his death in 1996.
studyNotes: Off-the-shelf parts, strict rules. He used only standard tubes and fixtures; the creativity is in placement, colour and dedication.
The light spills beyond the object. The tubes are the source, but the work is the coloured space and wall they produce. Notice where colours mix.
Corners and corridors. He often used architectural edges to split and frame the light, turning a room into the composition.
Titles as dedications. Each piece names a person or an event; the industrial material is given a personal address.
